newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Nomura convinced wrongdoing not systemic.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Nomura convinced wrongdoing not systemic.

text.p: Masashi Suzuki, president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, said on Tuesday he was convinced that a scandal involving suspected illegal deals was not systemic in the company.
However, Suzuki told Reuters in an interview that regulators would decide if Nomura itself was involved in wrongdoing.

"While our company executives were involved in (the scandal), we are convinced that it was not systemic (in Nomura)," Suzuki said. However, he added: "We will await for the outcome of investigations and judgement by regulators."

He also said that the scandal, revealed by Nomura on March 6, would have severe impact on its business results in the current financial year which started on April 1, while it had little impact on results for last business year.
"We don't know exactly how severe the impact on earnings will be because it is not known whether and how much administrative punishment will be imposed," Suzuki said.

On March 6 Nomura announced that an internal probe had found that two of its directors had been involved in apparently illegal deals which involved transferring money from a Nomura account to a corporate client's account.
Japanese prosecutors and officials of the securities watchdog have been investigating the payments that were made to a company run by a relative of a racketeer.

Suzuki, who added the post of president to his position as chairman on March 14 when former president Hideo Sakamaki stepped down over the scandal, said that his top priority was to restore trust in the company.

He said he would take all possible steps to avoid any recurrence of wrongdoing at the company. He said Nomura would establish a compliance committee made up of senior executives. The company president would chair the committee, he said.
"There are other measures we are considering," Suzuki said.
"By taking such measures, which issuers and investors are carefully watching, we can again become the securities house of choice," he said.
He also said he did not see any possibility that the scandal would delay implementation of "Big Bang" reforms to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001.

To boost international competitiveness, Suzuki said Nomura was considering setting up a holding company with the securities house as its core firm. The new setup would offer a variety of financial services, he said.
Nomura would aim to offer value-added financial services to maintain its positions in the face of the Big Bang reforms, Suzuki said.

He said that while expected liberalisation of stockbroking commissions would put pressure on Nomura's earnings, lifting various regulations on securities markets would also offer it opportunities to expand its business.
